title: Bunching
intro: This square is not a room: it is two particles on one line. Across is the position x₁ of particle 1, down is the position x₂ of particle 2, and ψ(x₁, x₂) is one wave for the pair. The particles are identical bosons, so ψ is symmetric under swapping them (the mirror image across the dashed diagonal). They fly at each other and meet a thin wall at x = 20, which each passes or bounces off: the wall is a beam splitter for both at once, and in this picture it is a cross. Green squares: both particles end up on the same side. Red: one on each side. Tune the speed.
goal: Choose the speed so that both particles always leave on the same side of the wall (green), never one on each side (red). Each particle's own speed is |k₀|/√2. Observe from t = 5: the observation finds both particles at once, a point (x₁, x₂).

physics.point: Two ways to end up on opposite sides: both pass, or both bounce. For identical bosons these two histories are the same final state, and at a 50/50 wall their amplitudes cancel. The particles always leave together.

idea: In 1987 Hong, Ou and Mandel sent two identical photons into the two inputs of a 50/50 beam splitter at the same moment. Classical particles, and distinguishable quantum ones, leave by different outputs half the time. The photons never did: they always left together. The dip in coincidences is now the standard test that two photons are truly indistinguishable, and the elementary step of photonic quantum computing.

The trick of this level: one particle in two dimensions obeys the same equation as two particles in one dimension. The grid's x is particle 1's position, y is particle 2's, and ψ(x, y) is the joint wave function. The wall at x = 20 on the line becomes a vertical bar (for particle 1) and a horizontal bar (for particle 2): a cross. A point that the Born rule picks is both particles' positions at once.

Bosons make ψ symmetric under exchange, so the launch is two mirror-image packets. They meet at the centre of the cross. The pair can leave on opposite sides in two ways, both transmitted or both reflected, and for identical bosons these two ways end in the same state: their amplitudes t² and r² add. A symmetric wall makes r and t a quarter cycle apart in phase, so t² + r² = T − R, which is zero for a 50/50 wall.
maths: With transmission and reflection amplitudes t and r of the wall (T = |t|², R = |r|², T + R = 1), the probability of one particle on each side is

maths.eq:
bosons:            |t² + r²|²  = (T − R)²
distinguishable:   |t²|² + |r²|² = T² + R²
fermions:          |t² − r²|²  = (T + R)² = 1

maths: The wall's transmission grows with speed, and T = ½ at a particle speed of about 1.8 (|k₀| ≈ 2.55). There bosons almost always leave together:

Distinguishable particles never do better than 50%. Fermions do the opposite, leaving on opposite sides nearly always (about 24% together here, the rest from the packets' speed spread): they cannot both be in the same place, the exclusion principle drawn as the empty diagonal.
try: Watch the diagonal: ψ is mirror-symmetric across it all the time, because the particles are identical.
At the default speed the wall mostly reflects (R > T): many runs end red.
Set |k₀| ≈ 2.55: after the cross, all the probability sits in the two green squares.
